common_name: Lilac Wonder Dog's-Tooth Violet (RHS Award Rosy-Lilac Trout Lily)

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil under deciduous shade; this old selection carries a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit for its reliability and depth of color.

directions: Set the elongated, tooth-shaped corms 2-3 inches deep in fall into cool, humus-rich soil beneath deciduous trees, then leave the colony undisturbed to slowly bulk up. This long-grown selection, honored with an Award of Merit decades ago and still carrying the RHS Award of Garden Merit, opens rich imperial-lilac, reflexed flowers over a chocolate-brown central zone, held above the species' characteristic brown-marbled leaves. Bloom comes in earliest spring and foliage disappears by early summer, so interplant with later-emerging ferns or hostas to cover the gap. Avoid summer irrigation once the leaves yellow, since the dormant corms resent wet soil during their rest period.
sources: Alpine Garden Society Encyclopaedia of Plants

common_name: Snowflake Dog's-Tooth Violet (Blush-White Mottled-Leaf Trout Lily)

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil under deciduous shade; this selected clone carries near-white flowers rather than the species' usual pink-to-lilac range.

directions: Plant corms in autumn in cool, leafy woodland soil, siting the colony where it will go undisturbed for years as it slowly multiplies. Snowflake stands apart from most dens-canis forms by opening blush-white, strongly reflexed flowers with contrasting blue anthers above the species' usual brown-mottled foliage, a cooler counterpoint to the more common rose and lilac shades. It is an early, fleeting bloomer, dying back to dormancy by late spring, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the corms while they rest. Divide congested clumps immediately after flowering if increase is wanted, replanting at once since the corms dislike prolonged drying.
sources: Alpine Garden Society Encyclopaedia of Plants

common_name: Pink Perfection Dog's-Tooth Violet (Pastel Pink Mottled-Leaf Trout Lily)

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil under deciduous shade; this clone is valued for its clear, soft pastel-pink flowers, a gentler shade than the species' usual deeper rose-lilac tones.

directions: Set corms 2-3 inches deep in autumn into rich, well-drained woodland soil beneath deciduous cover, then let the colony establish undisturbed for the best long-term display. Pink Perfection bears delicate pastel-pink, swept-back flowers over the species' signature brown-and-silver mottled foliage, a softer palette next to the more saturated lilac and purple selections of the species. Like all dens-canis forms it is an early-spring ephemeral that vanishes completely by early summer, so pair it with later-leafing companions that can mask the bare ground it leaves behind. Established colonies increase slowly by offset corms and self-sown seed under good woodland conditions.
sources: Alpine Garden Society Encyclopaedia of Plants

common_name: Frans Hals Dog's-Tooth Violet (Historic Violet-Purple Trout Lily)

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil under deciduous shade; this is one of the oldest named dens-canis selections still in cultivation, tracing back to plants grown in Europe since the sixteenth century.

directions: Plant corms in fall in cool, humus-rich woodland soil beneath deciduous trees, choosing a site that stays undisturbed for years as the colony slowly bulks up. One of the longest-cultivated forms of the species, Frans Hals opens violet-purple, strongly reflexed flowers with a yellow ring encircling the throat, set above the typical brown-marbled foliage. Its early bloom and complete summer dormancy follow the same seasonal rhythm as the wild species, so site it where neighboring plants can fill the space once the leaves die back. The long garden history of this selection speaks to its reliability and persistence when given well-drained, humus-rich conditions.
sources: Alpine Garden Society Encyclopaedia of Plants

planting.note: Plant in ordinary garden soil in partial to full shade; Silverwood is the first white-flowered selection of the species and tolerates dry shade beneath trees better than most white perennials.

directions: Plant in average, even dry, garden soil in full to partial shade, where it spreads gradually by rhizomes and self-sown seedlings to form a weed-smothering patch beneath trees and shrubs. Named for the Hampshire garden that holds the national collection of the species, Silverwood was selected as the first pure white-flowered form of the knotted cranesbill, its cup-shaped blooms held above glossy, deeply lobed foliage from late spring into autumn. It is markedly more shade- and drought-tolerant than most hardy geraniums, making it useful for the difficult dry shade under mature trees where few flowering perennials persist. Cut back hard after the first flush of bloom to encourage a tidy reflush of foliage and a second round of flowers.

common_name: Royal Robe Sweet Violet (Fragrant Violet-Blue Woodland Violet)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring into moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Royal Robe is grown chiefly for its intensely fragrant, silky violet-blue flowers with small white eyes.

directions: Plant divisions in fall or early spring into evenly moist, humus-rich soil at a shaded woodland edge, where the spreading rosettes knit together into a low, fragrant carpet. Royal Robe produces abundant violet-blue flowers with small white centers over heart-shaped foliage, their heavy perfume carrying well beyond the planting on still, cool days. It spreads steadily by short runners and self-sown seed, making it a useful shaded groundcover beneath shrubs or along a shaded path where its scent can be appreciated at close range. Lift and divide congested clumps every few years in fall to maintain vigorous flowering and prevent the center of the patch from thinning out.

common_name: Queen Charlotte Sweet Violet (Lavender-Blue Shade Violet)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring into moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; this heirloom selection dates to around 1900 and forms a dense, low clump of intensely fragrant lavender-blue flowers.

directions: Set divisions into cool, humus-rich soil at a shaded path edge or beneath deciduous shrubs, where this compact heirloom knits into a dense low mound of heart-shaped leaves. First introduced around the turn of the twentieth century, Queen Charlotte bears intensely perfumed, lavender-blue flowers held just above the foliage over a long late-winter-into-spring season. Its tight, non-invasive habit makes it a better choice than the wild species for container culture or small shaded borders where a more sprawling violet would be unwelcome. Top-dress with compost each fall to keep the shallow-rooted clump vigorous through winter.

common_name: Alba Sweet Violet (White-Flowered Fragrant Woodland Violet)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring into moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; Alba is the classic white-flowered color form of the fragrant sweet violet.

directions: Plant divisions in fall or early spring into evenly moist, humus-rich soil beneath deciduous trees or shrubs, where the low rosettes spread gradually by stolons into an informal shaded groundcover. Alba carries the same sweet, carrying fragrance as the wild violet-blue species but opens pure white flowers instead, a useful brightening note for a shaded nook or woodland path edge. Both flowers and young leaves are edible, the blooms traditionally crystallized for confectionery or floated in drinks. Divide crowded patches every two to three years in fall to keep flowering strong and refresh the planting.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Clive Groves Sweet Violet (Vigorous Deep Purple Reblooming Violet)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall or early spring into moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; introduced in 1985 by the Groves violet nursery in Dorset, this vigorous selection often produces a light repeat bloom in fall.

directions: Plant divisions into humus-rich, evenly moist soil in a partially to fully shaded spot, giving this robust selection room to spread into a dense, floriferous patch. Clive Groves bears extremely fragrant, deep purple flowers touched with violet over vigorous heart-shaped foliage, and unlike many sweet violet cultivars it often produces a light second flush of bloom in autumn alongside its main spring display. Its strong constitution makes it more forgiving of average garden conditions than some of the more delicate historic violet cultivars. Divide and replant congested clumps in fall every few years to sustain bloom quality.

common_name: Marie Louise Parma Violet (Historic Double Lavender Fragrant Violet)

planting.note: Plant divisions in a sheltered, partially shaded spot with rich, moist, well-drained soil; this double-flowered Parma violet, grown since about 1865, is less cold-hardy than common sweet violet and benefits from winter protection or cold-frame culture in colder regions.

directions: Grow in a sheltered, partially shaded border or cold frame with rich, moist, well-drained soil, since this old Parma violet strain is considerably more tender than common sweet violet and dislikes hard freezes or waterlogged winter soil. Marie Louise, in cultivation since the Victorian era, bears small, intensely fragrant, fully double flowers in soft lavender over neat mounds of rounded foliage, historically prized for the cut-flower and perfume trade. In colder climates it performs best lifted into pots for winter protection or grown against a warm, sheltered wall. Divide carefully in spring after the main flush of bloom to maintain vigor, since old clumps can lose vigor if left undisturbed too long.

planting.note: Plant in consistently moist, humus-rich soil at a pond or stream edge in partial shade to full sun; this German-raised selection, trialled at RHS Wisley since 1928, bears deep golden-orange globe flowers.

directions: Plant in reliably moist, humus-rich soil beside a pond, stream, or rain garden, where consistent moisture keeps the clump lush through summer. Feuertroll, also sold under the English name Fireglobe, opens deep golden-orange, tightly cupped flowers on upright stems above dark green, finely cut foliage in mid-spring. One of the older named globeflower hybrids still widely grown, it holds its rich color better in cool weather and in light shade than in hot, dry sun. Divide every three to four years in fall or early spring to maintain a tight, floriferous clump and to prevent the center from dying out.

common_name: Earliest of All Globeflower (Early-Blooming Buttercup-Yellow Globeflower)

planting.note: Plant in soil that never fully dries out, such as a bog, pond margin, or damp meadow, in partial shade to full sun; this selection is valued for blooming earlier than other globeflower cultivars.

directions: Site in constantly damp, humus-rich soil at a bog garden, pond margin, or low spot that never fully dries out, since dry soil quickly stunts and stresses this moisture-loving perennial. True to its name, Earliest of All opens large, buttercup-yellow globe-shaped flowers on sturdy stems in mid-spring, ahead of most other globeflower selections, giving an early season lift to a damp shaded border. Its upright habit and cut-flower-worthy stems make it useful both in the ground and in the vase. Lift and divide every few years in fall to rejuvenate the clump and maintain strong early bloom.
